Data Centers Are the Growth Engine of America’s Power Grid
 
Plus, Nvidia is the central bank to AI’s circular economy and bad school photos
 
 
UNCREDITED
 

Backlash against data-center construction is raising questions about the future of America’s AI build-out. For the power grid, the picture isn’t as murky—data centers are by far the biggest growth engine.

 

They are vacuuming up electricity at a historic clip, ending decades of static power usage and reshaping who is plugging into the grid.

 

Nationally, electricity use by commercial customers—a broad category that includes data centers—is poised to surpass residential demand this year for the first time, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

 

Data centers for artificial intelligence, cloud computing and cryptocurrency mining, as well as offices and shopping centers, fall in the EIA’s commercial division. Residential and industrial—including things like factories, refineries and agriculture—are the other big categories.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Is Anthropic Worth $1.1 Trillion, or $1.5 Trillion? How to Make Sense of the Valuations

 

As investors start to trade the AI company’s shares, they may encounter some very different market-capitalization figures, depending on what source they are using.

 
 
 

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

The United Arab Emirates’ economy is expected to grow 7.3% in 2027 after expanding just 0.2% this year, assuming regional disruptions ease, the International Monetary Fund says. The Middle East conflict affected hydrocarbon production and key nonoil sectors during the second quarter, although oil output has since recovered. Hydrocarbon growth is projected at 13.3% next year, compared with 2.3% in 2026, while nonoil activity is expected to grow 5.4% after contracting 0.5% this year. Inflation is forecast to ease to around 3% in 2027 from 5% this year. The IMF expects the country’s fiscal surplus to narrow to near balance in 2026 before recovering next year, while its current-account surplus is also projected to shrink significantly amid disruptions to trade and travel. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

 

Despite recent analysis suggesting that France’s economic woes are overblown, its public finances remain under significant pressure, Andrew Kenningham at Oxford Economics says in a note. “If our forecasts are accurate, France would need to run a broadly balanced primary budget by 2030 if its debt is to be on a stable trajectory at that point,” Kenningham says. With a deficit of around 3% of GDP expected this year, an adjustment of 3% of GDP will be required by 2030. This is unlikely without significant external pressure, for example from the bond market, he says. An improvement in global markets, a rebound in French GDP or reassuring plans from the next government could ease concerns. “But the arithmetic itself is definitely worrying.” (don.forbes@wsj.com)
